newsitem.title: CHINA: Rain could still dampen Sino-German ties - Herzog.
newsitem.headline: Rain could still dampen Sino-German ties - Herzog.

text.p: German President Roman Herzog said in Beijing on Tuesday he raised human rights issues in talks with his Chinese counterpart and warned that stormy weather could still lash Sino-German ties.
"I mentioned the themes of human rights and the rule of law," Herzog said of his meeting with Chinese President Jiang Zemin in the Great Hall of the People.
In a news briefing after the meeting, Herzog quoted Jiang as saying Sino-German relations had improved markedly with a visit by German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel last month.
"He said after rain there will be sunshine," Herzog quoted Jiang as saying. "I told him after sunshine it can rain again," Herzog said.
"I told him we have to work together so that there will be no rain clouds," he said, but did not elaborate.
During a visit to China last month that was long-delayed by a dispute over Tibet, Kinkel said China and Germany had shelved their differences and set a course for expanded economic ties.
Herzog said he brought up specific human rights cases with the Chinese president, adding that he and Jiang discussed human rights for about 15 minutes of their hour-long meeting.
He gave no details of the content of the talks.

The two presidents also signed an agreement for Germany to provide 180 million marks ($120 million) in credit to China for environmental projects, such as waste water treatment and clean coal-burning technology.
Herzog said Jiang had briefed him on domestic Chinese issues, such as Beijing's market-oriented economic reforms and China's huge population.
The German president has been under pressure at home to stress human rights in ties with Beijing after a recent crackdown on dissent by China's communist rulers.
A Beijing court last week rejected the appeal of dissident and former student leader Wang Dan and upheld his 11-year jail term for plotting to subvert the government.
The sentence was the latest in a series of blows to China's struggling democracy movement.
